## Limitations of GANs

@fig-gan-geometry is the lecture's geometric picture of a GAN [@gdl]. A latent distribution $\nu$ on a latent space $\mathcal{Y}$ is pushed by the generator $G_\theta$ into the data space $\mathcal{X}$, and $\theta$ is chosen to bring the result close to the data distribution $\mu$,

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathrm{dist}(\mu_\theta,\mu)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad\mu_\theta = G_{\theta\#}\nu .
$$

![The geometry of a GAN. The latent space $\mathcal{Y}$ carries the prior $\nu$, drawn as a cloud of samples; the generator $G_\theta$ carries it into the data space $\mathcal{X}$ as the push-forward $\mu_\theta = G_{\theta\#}\nu$, the shaded ellipse, and training moves $\mu_\theta$ towards the data distribution $\mu$, whose samples are the face grid. The distance between the two is what the discriminator estimates. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion].](figures/lec08/slide39-gan-geometry.png){#fig-gan-geometry width=80%}

The distance is not computed directly but estimated by the discriminator, which turns training into a min-max game. @fig-mode-collapse shows what can go wrong when $\mu$ has several modes. The pushforward $\mu_\theta$ settles on one of them and misses the others, which is called mode collapse. Two effects contribute. A continuous $G_\theta$ maps a connected latent space onto a connected set, so it cannot cover well-separated modes without also putting mass between them. In addition, the adversarial game lets the generator stay on whichever modes the discriminator currently accepts.

![Mode collapse, the same picture with a multi-modal $\mu$. The data distribution now has two groups of faces, drawn as two clusters inside $\mathcal{X}$, and the single push-forward $\mu_\theta$ covers one of them. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion].](figures/lec08/slide40-mode-collapse.png){#fig-mode-collapse width=80%}

The lecture calls the second weakness GAN overfitting, and it is visible in editing. GAN-based editing methods first invert an image to a latent code, and even their reconstructions lose a hand held in front of the face, or the details of a building [@kim2022diffusionclip]. Most training faces are frontal and unoccluded, so inverting and regenerating projects the image onto a range that is dominated by the majority of the data. Deterministic DDIM, on the other hand, follows an ODE flow (@eq-pf-sigma) and can be inverted almost exactly by iterating $x_{t+1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t+1}}\hat{x}_t+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t+1}}\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$, which is why DiffusionCLIP keeps the hand. @fig-gan-scale-space puts the two pictures side by side.

The third weakness is in @fig-single-step: a GAN is a single-step sampler. The network has to represent the entire map from noise to data, and a sample comes from one pass through it, so there is no intermediate state at which an error could be corrected.

![A GAN as the lecture draws its training and its sampling. Above, samples from the data distribution train the network; below, one pass through the trained generator produces a sample. The whole map from the latent prior to the data is carried by that single step. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion].](figures/lec08/slide42-single-step.png){#fig-single-step width=85%}

![(a) A GAN learns one push-forward $\mu_\theta = G_{\theta\#}\nu$ from the latent prior $\nu$ on $\mathcal{Y}$ into the data space; when $\mu$ has separated modes a continuous $G_\theta$ cannot cover them all, which is mode collapse (@fig-gan-geometry, @fig-mode-collapse). (b) Forward diffusion instead builds a scale-space $p_t = p_0 * \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_t^2I)$ in which the modes merge into one well-conditioned distribution, and reverse Langevin dynamics transports samples back down the scales along $\nabla\log p_t$ (@fig-dmcmc, @fig-score-field). The chapter's argument is that the second picture has intermediate states and the first does not.](figures/lec07/deb-kit2-fig4-gan-vs-scale-space.png){#fig-gan-scale-space width=100%}

## Scale-space in the distribution domain

Scale-space theory (@fig-scale-space-theory) represents a signal $f$ at all scales $t\ge0$ by blurring it with a Gaussian,

$$
L_t = h_t*f,\qquad h_t(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi t)^{n/2}}e^{-\Vert x\Vert^2/2t}.
$$ {#eq-scale-space}

![Scale-space on an image, as the lecture introduces it. The same photograph is shown as $L(\cdot,\cdot;t) = g(\cdot,\cdot;t)*f$ at $t=0,1,4$ and $16$: fine structure disappears as the scale grows, and nothing new appears. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion].](figures/lec08/slide44-scale-space-theory.png){#fig-scale-space-theory width=95%}

The Gaussian is the only kernel that satisfies the scale-space axioms [@koenderink1984; @lindeberg1994], namely linearity, shift invariance, the semigroup property $h_s*h_t = h_{s+t}$, rotational symmetry, and non-enhancement of local extrema (maxima never increase and minima never decrease, and in one dimension no new extrema appear). Moving to coarser scales smooths away fine structure.

The slides state that uniqueness without proof [@koenderink1984; @lindeberg1994]. Two of the axioms are used directly later, so we record them.

::: {#prp-heat}
## The Gaussian scale-space solves the heat equation
For $t>0$, $\partial_t h_t = \tfrac12\Delta h_t$, and hence $L_t = h_t*f$ satisfies $\partial_tL_t = \tfrac12\Delta L_t$ for bounded continuous $f$, with $L_t\to f$ as $t\to0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $r = \Vert x\Vert$, $\log h_t = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log(2\pi t)-r^2/2t$ gives $\partial_th_t = \big(-\tfrac{n}{2t}+\tfrac{r^2}{2t^2}\big)h_t$, while $\partial_i^2h_t = \big(-\tfrac1t+\tfrac{x_i^2}{t^2}\big)h_t$, so $\tfrac12\Delta h_t = \tfrac12\big(-\tfrac{n}{t}+\tfrac{r^2}{t^2}\big)h_t = \partial_th_t$. The derivatives are integrable and $f$ is bounded, so they pass inside the convolution by dominated convergence. As $t\to0$ the density $h_t$ concentrates at the origin, so $h_t*f\to f$ at every point of continuity.
:::

::: {#prp-semigroup}
## Semigroup property
$h_s*h_t = h_{s+t}$ for all $s,t>0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The Fourier transform of $h_t$ is $e^{-t\Vert\omega\Vert^2/2}$ and takes convolution to multiplication; the product of the transforms for $s$ and $t$ is the transform for $s+t$, and the transform is injective on integrable functions.
:::

For two modes one can say exactly when the blur merges them, which is the mechanism the whole argument rests on.

::: {#prp-merge}
## When two Gaussian modes merge
Let $p_0 = \tfrac12\mathcal{N}(-m,s^2)+\tfrac12\mathcal{N}(m,s^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $m>0$. Then $p_t = \tfrac12\mathcal{N}(-m,v)+\tfrac12\mathcal{N}(m,v)$ with $v = s^2+t$, and $p_t$ is bimodal if and only if $m^2>v$. The modes merge at the critical scale $t^\star = m^2-s^2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @prp-semigroup the convolution acts on each component, giving the stated $p_t$. Up to a constant $p_t\propto e_1+e_2$ with $e_{1,2} = e^{-(x\mp m)^2/2v}$. Setting the derivative to zero and using $e_1/e_2 = e^{2mx/v}$ gives $x(e_1+e_2) = m(e_1-e_2)$, that is $x = m\tanh(mx/v)$. Zero is always a solution; the right-hand side is odd, concave on $x>0$, bounded by $m$, and has slope $m^2/v$ at the origin, so a nonzero solution exists exactly when $m^2/v>1$, and then $x=0$ is the minimum between two maxima.
:::

![The scale-space of a bimodal density loses a mode at exactly the critical scale $t^\star = m^2-s^2$ of @prp-merge. Left: $p_t(x)$ over $(x,t)$ for $m=2$, $s=0.5$, with the local maxima in red merging at the dashed line $t^\star = 3.75$. Right: slices at four scales, the dashed one at $t^\star$ flat at the top.](figures/lec08/Kwak-MJ-scalespace-1d.png){#fig-mode-merge width=100%}

The count of modes therefore falls as the scale grows, which is "no new extrema" in its one-dimensional form, and @fig-mode-merge shows a sampler's reason for climbing the scale-space: above $t^\star$ there is one mode to find, and the two are recovered on the way back down.

Slide 45 recalls the density of a sum of independent random variables. For independent $X$ and $Y$ with densities $f_X$ and $f_Y$, we have $F_{X+Y}(a) = \int\!\int_{-\infty}^{a-y}f_X(x)f_Y(y)\,dx\,dy = \int F_X(a-y)f_Y(y)\,dy$, and differentiating in $a$ gives

$$
f_{X+Y}(a) = \int f_X(a-y)\,f_Y(y)\,dy = (f_X*f_Y)(a).
$$ {#eq-conv}

Applying @eq-conv to the VE step $x_t = x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\sigma_t^2-\sigma_{t-1}^2}\,z$ gives

$$
p_t = p_{t-1}*h_{\sigma_t^2-\sigma_{t-1}^2} = p_0*h_{\sigma_t^2},
$$ {#eq-dist-scale-space}

where the second equality follows from the semigroup property with $\sigma_0 = 0$. The forward process is the scale-space of @eq-scale-space applied to the density $p_0$, at scale $\sigma_t^2$. The lecture writes the first equality as $p(x_{t-1}) = p(x_t)*h(x_t)$, with its time index reversed. For VP the same holds after rescaling $x$ by $1/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$. @fig-dmcmc shows why this is useful. Separate modes merge at coarse scales, where a sampler can move between them before following the scales back down. Its lower panels compare running the reverse SDE or ODE from pure noise at $\sigma=348$, which often fails to produce a clean face, with starting it from an MCMC chain run at much lower noise levels ($\sigma$ between 1.41 and 2.03), which gives clean faces.

![The scale-space of the distribution. Above, the density over the data space at three noise levels, $\sigma$ increasing down the left axis: the data density at the back has separate sharp modes, and they broaden and merge as $\sigma$ grows, which is where the green MCMC chain crosses from one mode to another before the reverse S/ODE (dashed) carries the sample back to the data level. Below, samples: starting the reverse SDE or ODE from pure noise at $\sigma=348$ (left) often fails, while starting from an MCMC chain at $\sigma$ between $1.41$ and $2.03$ (right) gives clean faces. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @kim2023dmcmc.](figures/lec08/slide43-scale-space-distribution.png){#fig-dmcmc width=90%}

## Iterative denoising as the dual representation

The convolution in @eq-dist-scale-space acts on densities. On samples, the same operation simply adds i.i.d. noise to every pixel. The lecture puts the two side by side as $p(x_{t-1}) = p(x_t)*p(\sigma_t\epsilon_t)$ and $x_{t-1} = x_t+\sigma_t\epsilon_t$, again with the time index reversed, and calls the second the dual representation of the first. What moves the samples is the score, @fig-score-field. Undoing a convolution of densities is an ill-posed deconvolution problem, but on samples it becomes iterative denoising guided by the score. One example is Langevin dynamics,

$$
x_{i+1}\leftarrow x_i+\delta\,\nabla_{x}\log p(x_i)+\sqrt{2\delta}\,z_i,\qquad i=0,1,\dots,K,
$$ {#eq-langevin}

which we write with step size $\delta$ because $\epsilon$ already denotes the noise (the lecture uses $\epsilon$). @sec-fp explains why this procedure samples from $p$ when the step size is small and the number of steps is large.

![The animation the lecture plays for the reverse direction, at its first and last frame. The contours are level sets of a density with several modes, the arrows are $\nabla\log p$, which points towards the nearest mode everywhere, and the blue dots are samples. (a) The samples start on a grid, spread over the whole plane. (b) After the Langevin chain of @eq-langevin has run, each has followed the arrows onto a mode, and what is left is a sample of $p$. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after the blog post accompanying @sde.](figures/lec08/slide46-score-field.png){#fig-score-field width=95%}

## The Gaussian shell theorem and the hypercylinder

::: {#thm-shell}
## Gaussian shell theorem
Let $X = (X_1,\dots,X_n)$ have i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ entries. Then $\Vert X\Vert^2/n\to\sigma^2$ in probability, so $\Vert X\Vert\approx\sigma\sqrt n$ and the mass concentrates on the sphere of radius $\sigma\sqrt n$ (@fig-chi2).
:::

::: {.proof}
We have $\mathbb{E}\Vert X\Vert^2 = n\sigma^2$ and $\mathrm{Var}\Vert X\Vert^2 = n\,\mathrm{Var}(X_i^2) = 2n\sigma^4$. By Chebyshev's inequality, $P(|\Vert X\Vert^2/n-\sigma^2|>r)\le2\sigma^4/(nr^2)$, which tends to zero. This is the law of large numbers mentioned in the lecture. Since the square root is continuous, $\Vert X\Vert/\sqrt n\to\sigma$.
:::

The relative width of the shell shrinks like $1/\sqrt{2n}$, while its absolute width tends to the constant $\sigma/\sqrt2$ [@vershynin2018]: for a $256\times256\times3$ image the shell is about $0.16\%$ of its own radius thick, which is why it is drawn as a surface rather than a region. The $\chi^2$ curves of @fig-chi2 and panel (a) of @fig-shell show the same concentration.

![The Gaussian shell theorem as the lecture states it. Left: the mass of an isotropic Gaussian sits on a sphere, not at the origin. Right: the density of $\chi^2_\nu/\nu$ for $\nu = 1, 2, 4, 10, 30, 100$; as the dimension grows the curve concentrates at $1$, which is $\Vert X\Vert^2/n\to\sigma^2$. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @chung2022mcg.](figures/lec08/slide47-gaussian-shell.png){#fig-chi2 width=85%}

The density of $X$ is nevertheless largest at the origin, and the two statements are reconciled by the radial density. Writing $R = \Vert X\Vert$ and integrating over the sphere,

$$
f_R(r)\propto r^{n-1}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2},\qquad r\ge0,
$$ {#eq-radial}

whose maximum for $n>1$ is at $r = \sigma\sqrt{n-1}$. The Cartesian density falls off from the origin, but the volume factor $r^{n-1}$ grows faster until that radius, and in high dimension the product is sharply peaked there. The concentration is an asymptotic statement and not a small-$n$ one: a simulation at $n=3$ puts $\mathbb{E}\Vert X\Vert/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ at about $0.94$, still noticeably below one.

The lecture then considers data lying on a $k$-dimensional linear subspace $V$, perturbed by noise with $p(y\mid x) = \mathcal{N}(x,\sigma^2I)$. Write $y = x+\sigma z$ and let $P_\perp$ be the projection onto the orthogonal complement of $V$. Since $P_\perp x=0$, the distance from $y$ to $V$ is $\Vert P_\perp y\Vert = \sigma\Vert P_\perp z\Vert$. Here $P_\perp z$ is a standard Gaussian in $n-k$ dimensions, so @thm-shell gives

$$
\mathrm{dist}(y,V)\approx\sigma\sqrt{n-k}.
$$ {#eq-cylinder}

The component along $V$ is unconstrained, so $p(y)$ concentrates on a hypercylinder of radius $\sigma\sqrt{n-k}$ around $V$, as panel (b) of @fig-shell shows. Here the approximation can be replaced by an exact law: $P_\perp z$ is standard Gaussian in $n-k$ dimensions, so

$$
\frac{\mathrm{dist}(y,V)^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-k}
$$ {#eq-chisq}

exactly, for every $n$ and $k$, and @eq-cylinder is its concentration. The same calculation also factorises the noisy density itself: with $P$ the projection onto $V$,

$$
p(y) = \big(p*\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I_k)\big)(Py)\cdot(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-(n-k)/2}e^{-\Vert P_\perp y\Vert^2/2\sigma^2},
$$

a blurred copy of the data density along $V$ times a fixed Gaussian across it. The noise is doing two different things in the two directions, and only the second is the shell.

![(a) The norm of an $n$-dimensional standard Gaussian divided by $\sqrt n$, which concentrates at 1 as $n$ grows. (b) The distance to a $k$-dimensional subspace after adding $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ noise in $n=1000$ dimensions. It concentrates at $\sqrt{n-k}$ (dashed lines) with the same width for every $k$.](figures/lec07/HaJunHyun-shell.png){#fig-shell width=100%}

## Transitions between noisy manifolds {#sec-manifold}

Locally, a curved data manifold $\mathcal{M}$ of dimension $k$ looks like a subspace. As long as the tube radius $\sigma_i\sqrt{n-k}$ is small compared with the radius of curvature of $\mathcal{M}$, @eq-cylinder implies that samples at noise level $\sigma_i$ lie in a thin tube

$$
\mathcal{M}_i = \{y\mid\mathrm{dist}(y,\mathcal{M})\approx\sigma_i\sqrt{n-k}\}
$$

around $\mathcal{M}$ (@fig-noisy-tube, after @chung2022mcg). For the VP process, $\mathcal{M}_i$ surrounds $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\,\mathcal{M}$ at radius $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\sqrt{n-k}$. The noise levels give a sequence of thin shells $\mathcal{M}_1,\mathcal{M}_2,\dots,\mathcal{M}_\infty$ at increasing distance from $\mathcal{M}$. @fig-manifolds draws them as nested contours ending at $\mathcal{N}(a_\infty x_0,b_\infty^2I)$, where $a_\infty$ and $b_\infty$ are the limiting signal scale and noise level, and the lecture calls them discrete orbits.

![The tube at one noise level. The data manifold $\mathcal{M}$ is the inner curve; at noise level $\sigma_i$ the samples lie in the tube $\mathcal{M}_i$ around it, of radius $\sigma_i\sqrt{n-k}$, drawn as the circles swept along $\mathcal{M}$ and the outer envelope. The strip below shows one image carried out through the levels. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @chung2022mcg.](figures/lec08/slide49-noisy-tube.png){#fig-noisy-tube width=75%}

Forward diffusion moves outwards through these shells and reverse diffusion moves inwards.

![The nested noisy manifolds, reproduced from slide 50. Forward diffusion (red arrows) moves from the data manifold $\mathcal{M}$ out through the shells $\mathcal{M}_1,\dots,\mathcal{M}_i,\dots$ towards $\mathcal{N}(a_\infty x_0,b_\infty^2I)$, and reverse diffusion (blue arrows) moves back inwards.](figures/lec07/HaJunHyun-slide50-manifolds.png){#fig-manifolds width=60%}

The network at time $t$ has only been trained on inputs from $\mathcal{M}_t$. If a step misses the next shell, the network receives inputs it has never seen, and the error accumulates from step to step. This is the time-embedding remark of @fig-unet-time in geometric form. The decomposition of @fig-denoise-renoise, which is @eq-denoise-renoise again, is designed to avoid this. Tweedie's formula maps $x_t$ to the clean estimate $\hat{x}_t$, and the step then adds noise of total variance $1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$. When this noise behaves like an isotropic Gaussian, @thm-shell puts the result at the right distance, on $\mathcal{M}_{t-1}$. The lecture summarizes this as "retaining the correct manifold transition is the key". Landing on the right shell is necessary but not sufficient, since the renoise-only sampler of @tbl-toy does so at every step and is still biased. A GAN has no intermediate shells and must map $\nu$ onto $\mathcal{M}$ in a single step.

The same decomposition also holds in continuous time. In the variables of @eq-pf-sigma, the VP SDE becomes a VE SDE, because $d(x/\sqrt{\bar\alpha}) = \sqrt{\beta/\bar\alpha}\,dw$ and $d[\sigma^2]/dt = \beta/\bar\alpha$, and by @eq-epsilon-score-conversion its score is $-\epsilon^*/\sigma$. Tweedie's formula reads $\bar{x} = \hat{x}+\sigma\epsilon^*$ in these variables. One reverse Euler-Maruyama step from $\sigma$ to $\sigma'<\sigma$, as in @eq-ve-sampler, therefore gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{x}' &= \bar{x} - (\sigma^2-\sigma'^2)\frac{\epsilon^*}{\sigma} + \sqrt{\sigma^2-\sigma'^2}\,z\\
&= \underbrace{\hat{x}}_{\text{Tweedie's denoiser}} + \underbrace{\frac{\sigma'^2}{\sigma}\,\epsilon^*}_{\text{parametric noise}} + \underbrace{\sqrt{\sigma^2-\sigma'^2}\,z}_{\text{stochastic noise}},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-continuous-decomp}

while one Euler step of the probability flow ODE gives $\bar{x}' = \hat{x}+\sigma'\epsilon^*$ with no stochastic term. The reverse SDE step has the same three parts as @eq-ddim-step. Its parametric coefficient $\sigma'^2/\sigma$ is exactly that of $\eta=1$, while its stochastic coefficient differs only by the factor $\sigma/\sigma'$, which tends to one as the step becomes small compared with $\sigma'$. Its total noise variance $\sigma'^2+(\sigma^2-\sigma'^2)^2/\sigma^2$ matches the target $\sigma'^2$ up to second order in the step. In continuous time the probability flow ODE and the reverse SDE are the members $\eta=0$ and $\eta=1$ of the $\eta$ family.

## The Fokker-Planck equation {#sec-fp}

For a general SDE $dX_t = \mu(X_t,t)dt+\sigma(X_t,t)dW_t$ (slide 51), the density evolves according to

$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\big[\mu_i p\big] + \sum_{i,j=1}^n\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\big[D_{ij}p\big],\qquad D = \tfrac12\sigma\sigma^\top .
$$ {#eq-fp-general}

The SDE describes a single sample path, while @eq-fp-general describes the density, which is again the duality between samples and densities of @eq-langevin and @fig-score-field. With $\sigma = g(t)I$ we have $D = \frac12g^2I$ and recover @eq-fp.

Taking the Fourier transform in $x$ turns the Laplacian into multiplication by $-\Vert\omega\Vert^2$, so for a drift-free process with $D = \tfrac12g(t)^2I$ the equation becomes an ordinary differential equation in $t$ at each frequency,

$$
\partial_t\hat p(\omega,t) = -\tfrac12g(t)^2\Vert\omega\Vert^2\hat p(\omega,t),\qquad \hat p(\omega,t) = \hat p(\omega,0)\,e^{-v(t)\Vert\omega\Vert^2/2},\qquad v(t) = \int_0^tg(u)^2du .
$$ {#eq-fp-fourier}

The factor multiplying $\hat p(\omega,0)$ is the Fourier transform of $h_{v(t)}$, so inverting gives $p_t = p_0*h_{v(t)}$: the solution is the scale-space at scale $v(t)$, for any schedule $g$, which is @eq-dist-scale-space again with the time change made explicit.

Slide 52 treats the Wiener process. It takes $\mu=0$ and $D=I$, which means $\sigma=\sqrt2\,I$, and @eq-fp-general reduces to the heat equation $\partial_tp = \Delta p$. Its solution is $p(\cdot,t) = p(\cdot,0)*h_{2t}$ with $h_{2t}(x) = (4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-\Vert x\Vert^2/4t}$, because the Gaussian of @eq-scale-space satisfies $\partial_t h_t = \frac12\Delta h_t$. So the solution of the Fokker-Planck equation is the scale-space, as the slide says. The kernel written on the slide, $(2\pi t)^{-1/2}\exp(-\Vert x\Vert^2/2t^2)$, should be replaced by this one. For a standard Wiener process ($\sigma=I$, so $D=\frac12I$) the equation is $\partial_tp = \frac12\Delta p$ and the kernel is $h_t$ itself.

Slide 53 treats overdamped Langevin dynamics. It writes the SDE $dx = -\frac{1}{k_BT}\nabla U\,dt+dW$ together with the Fokker-Planck equation

$$
\partial_tp = \tfrac12\nabla\cdot\Big(\frac{p}{k_BT}\nabla U+\nabla p\Big).
$$

The flux vanishes when $\nabla\log p = -\nabla U/k_BT$, so the stationary density of this equation is $p\propto e^{-U/k_BT}$, which is the conclusion on the slide. The SDE and the equation do not quite match, however. With noise $dW$ we have $D=\frac12I$, and @eq-fp-general puts the factor $\frac12$ only on $\nabla p$, so the SDE exactly as written would have stationary density $e^{-2U/k_BT}$. The lines on the slide agree if the drift is halved, or if the noise is changed to $\sqrt2\,dW$, which doubles the right-hand side of the equation and leaves its stationary density unchanged. We use the second correction. Now set $k_BT=1$ and $U = -\log p_{\text{data}}$. The slide writes $U = \nabla\log p$ at this point, but the potential must be minus the log density. The stationary distribution is then $e^{-U} = p_{\text{data}}$, and the SDE becomes $dx = \nabla\log p_{\text{data}}\,dt+\sqrt2\,dW$, whose Euler-Maruyama step with step size $\delta$ is exactly @eq-langevin. With a small step size and many steps, Langevin dynamics samples the density at a single fixed scale. Reversing the whole scale-space requires either annealing over decreasing noise levels, as in SMLD, or the reverse SDE, and panel (b) of @fig-score shows why.

## Summary

Diffusion models are a scale-space of the data distribution, and iterative denoising is its dual representation on samples. The Gaussian shell theorem turns the noise levels into discrete orbits $\mathcal{M}_i$, and the continuous description is the Fokker-Planck equation, which for pure noise is the scale-space itself. A diffusion sampler relies on each reverse step staying on the correct manifold, which the denoise and renoise decomposition and a network that knows the noise level are designed to achieve. Single-step GANs have no such intermediate manifolds, and this is where diffusion models gain over them.
